newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German MPs urge Kohl to back EU jobs pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German MPs urge Kohl to back EU jobs pact.

text.p: A day after France stunned its European partners by putting the brakes on a key aspect of monetary union, Germany on Tuesday appeared ready to bend to French pressure and add a jobs chapter to the Maastricht treaty.

While the move is not entirely unexpected, it marks a shift in German policy, which has until now rejected any link between coordinated European Union efforts to boost employment and a stability pact aimed at guaranteeing the solidity of the euro.

Signalling the change in Germany's position, parliamentary deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats and Free Democrats urged the government to agree to include a jobs chapter in the so-called Maastricht II treaty.

"Fighting unemployment is a central task of the European Union and its member states," the coalition deputies said in a draft motion to be presented to parliament on Wednesday. "The federal government should agree to include a corresponding employment chapter in the treaty."
The deputies' motion also recommended that the EU Social Chapter be adopted in the Maastricht II treaty, which will be discussed at the EU summit in Amsterdam next week.

France's announcement on Monday that it could not yet approve the stability pact, coupled with Germany's budget woes, have thrown Europe's drive towards a single currency into disarray and raised doubts that monetary union will start on time.

It was expected that EU leaders would give final approval in Amsterdam to a stability pact -- the hard-fought deal which Germany hopes will ensure that EMU members maintain budget discipline after the single currency is launched in 1999.

The pact was agreed last December after a compromise between France and Germany. But the new French government is unhappy with the deal. It wants an ammendment to spell out how EU countries will coordinate economic policy after the launch of the euro.
Part of the treaty negotiations in Amsterdam will also include discussion of adopting a so-called Employment Chapter to make job creation a formal EU priority.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, speaking to Reuters Television after a meeting of his Free Democrats (FDP) party, said he thought Paris would accept the stability pact.
"France now needs some time after the elections," he said.

"But I have been clearly told that France is more concerned about the additional resolution than about the stability pact itself," he added. "I am convinced that France still wants the euro and the stability pact."

Helmut Haussmann, FDP European affairs expert, told Reuters the parliamentary groups of Kohl's CDU and sister party Christian Social Union (CSU) and the FDP had approved the draft statement in principle but would make a few make changes.

The motion would stress that any coordination of jobs policy would not require transferring any more authority to Brussels and would focus on easing unemployment through structural reforms under the responsibility of member states.
According to government officials who asked not to be identified, EU negotiations in Amsterdam will be largely concerned with the details of the Employment Chapter.

Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), whose support is required for passage of the Maastricht II treaty in parliament, dismissed the coalition's motion as an attempt to "put another empty title in the EU treaty".

"The federal government, faced with the opposition of all other European governments, is trying to turn the Employment Chapter into a farce," said Juergen Meyer, SPD European affairs spokesman in parliament.
